reasons: Rules are text matches, so they can pass or fail for reasons unrelated to security.
The sensitive data rule accepts any mention of the word sensitive in the upload view, which is a loose test.
Dependency audits are only listed in the report, not run by this script.

sections.name: File setup
sections.title: Setup and output location
sections.what: Sets the project root and the path of the security report file. It prepares the file for the rest of the script.
sections.why: Reason not stated in the code, though the report path matches the other verification outputs.
sections.watch_out: The script writes to build/verification, so that folder must be allowed to be created.

sections.name: _text
sections.title: Reading a project file as text
sections.what: Reads a named project file and returns its text, using UTF-8 encoding.
sections.why: Used by every rule that checks one specific file, so each check reads files the same way.
sections.watch_out: A wrong or renamed path makes the script crash before any rule is checked.

sections.name: _runtime_sources
sections.title: Collecting runtime source files
sections.what: Collects every Python, TypeScript, JavaScript, and HTML file in the backend, frontend source, and scripts folders, excluding this script itself.
sections.why: Likely reason: this script contains the search patterns, so scanning itself would cause false matches.
sections.watch_out: Only the frontend source folder is scanned, so files outside it are not checked by the broad rules.

sections.name: main (part 1)
sections.title: Running the security rules
sections.what: Reads the key source files and runs about eighteen rules covering local-only binding, upload limits, safe XML and spreadsheet handling, frozen dependency installs, content security policy, escaping, banned dynamic code, and secret leaks. It records each result.
sections.why: Likely reason: each rule guards a specific protection that a previous change or review wanted to keep.
sections.watch_out: The dynamic code rule looks for patterns like eval or innerHTML, so a harmless use of the same word could be flagged.

sections.name: main (part 2)
sections.title: Writing the report and failing on errors
sections.what: Lists the failed rules, writes the JSON report, and stops with an error naming any failed rule. If all rules pass, it prints the number of checks and files.
sections.why: Likely reason: the report must exist even when checks fail, so the release record shows the failure.
sections.watch_out: The report file is written before the failure is raised, so a file showing complete false can exist after a failed run.

sections.name: entry point
sections.title: Starting the script directly
sections.what: Runs the main function only when the file is started directly from the command line, not when it is imported.
sections.why: Standard Python pattern so other scripts can import this file without running the checks.

summary: Runs a set of about eighteen text-based security rules over the project's source files, writes a JSON report, and fails the build if any rule is broken.
purpose: Catches regressions in security settings, such as a server that listens on all network interfaces or an upload size limit that was removed.
why: Likely reason: the release gate must stop when a known security protection disappears. The script writes its report before it raises the failure, so the failure is recorded.
how: The script reads a fixed list of backend and frontend files, joins the source text of all runtime files, then runs each rule as a text or pattern match. It collects the names of failed rules, writes build/verification/security.json, and exits with an error if any rule failed. Otherwise it prints how many checks passed.
inputs: The project source files at fixed paths. No command line arguments.
outputs: The file build/verification/security.json with each check result, the list of failures, and the dependency audit commands. A pass or failure message in the terminal.
risks: Each rule is a text match, not a behaviour test. A rule passes if a phrase appears anywhere, even in an unused comment or dead code. A rule can also break simply because a file was renamed. The file is not a substitute for a real security review or the dependency audits.
debug: If a rule fails, open build/verification/security.json and find the name in the failures list. Then search the named file for the phrase the rule expects. If the script stops with a missing file error, a path in main has changed.
